claim: Brier is a strictly proper score: the forecaster's best expected score comes only from reporting true belief. Plain accuracy (zero-one) is not strictly proper and rewards rounding to 0 or 1.
agent_test: Score the agent's stated probabilities with Brier, not accuracy; check that rounding to 0/1 scores worse on a held-out class.

claim: The Brier skill score (1 - BS/BS_ref) is not strictly proper; its hedging gain vanishes only as the number of independent forecasts grows.
agent_test: Log raw Brier per class; compute skill only as a derived view. Simulate hedging on a 30-item class to size the gain.

claim: Mean Brier splits as REL - RES + UNC (Murphy 1973), with UNC = base rate x (1 - base rate). A useful forecast has Brier below UNC. The split is exact only for forecasts that take a finite set of values.
agent_test: Store REL, RES, UNC per class beside total Brier; check REL-RES+UNC equals the total on a discrete-value log.

claim: Binned decomposition and ECE estimates depend on the bin count and are biased. Bias-corrected versions reduce bias but have larger variance. A bin-free isotonic (CORP) version had the lowest MSE in the authors' simulations.
agent_test: On resolved items per class, compare 5-bin, 10-bin and CORP estimates by bootstrap; report counts and intervals.

claim: Brier has known blind spots: it can prefer a forecast that is certain and wrong (Jewson: f=0 beats f=0.25 by 1/80 when the event has frequency 0.1; arithmetic re-checked). A low Brier does not prove good calibration and only compares on the same question population.
agent_test: Pair Brier with a log-score or worst-case-miss count on the same items; compare class rankings. Do not compare Brier across classes with different base rates.

claim: Pretrained LLMs are well calibrated on lettered multiple choice via token probabilities. RLHF post-training breaks this: GPT-4 MMLU ECE 0.007 pre-trained vs 0.074 after; Kadavath found one fixed temperature (T=2.5) largely repairs RLHF policies.
agent_test: Fit one temperature on the class record of the chat model and measure ECE and Brier before/after on held-out items.

claim: A one-parameter temperature fit on held-out labelled data repairs most miscalibration in modern networks (CIFAR-100 ResNet-110 ECE 16.53% to 1.26%) but not everywhere (LeNet5 CIFAR-100 4.85% to 6.48%; Reuters 0.85% to 0.91%). It does not change discrimination.
agent_test: Same as K06; also test Platt vs temperature at several class-record sizes (30, 100, 300 items).
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: For RLHF chat models, stated (verbalized) probabilities are often better calibrated by ECE than token probabilities (gpt-3.5 TriviaQA 0.140 vs 0.068; GPT-4 0.078 vs 0.024), but Xiong et al. find verbalized confidence overconfident (80-100%, multiples of 5; average ECE above 0.377 for GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna). The two papers used different models, prompts and tasks. Gap-search note: Yang et al. 2026 re-ran both prompts side by side and found the Tian-style prompt better calibrated, especially for large models, so the conflict is mostly a prompt effect.
agent_test: On one fixed task set, compare token-probability, verbalized, and top-k verbalized confidence by ECE, AUROC and Brier at equal tokens.

claim: ECE alone can be gamed: a constant predictor can have near-perfect ECE (GPT-4 GSM8K ECE 0.064 by saying 100% at 93.6% accuracy; a 50% guesser has perfect binary ECE). Report a discrimination measure or Brier next to it.
agent_test: Log ECE with AUROC and Brier; flag any class where ECE is low and AUROC is near 0.5.

claim: Verbalized confidence from LLMs discriminates right from wrong weakly (GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7% across 8 tasks, Xiong). Sampling several answers and measuring agreement raises it a lot on some tasks (GSM8K AUROC 54.8% to 92.7%), but samples from one model are correlated.
agent_test: Compare AUROC of stated confidence vs agreement of 5 fresh-context samples on checked tasks at equal tokens; treat agreement as a hint (G4).

claim: Zero-shot LLMs without retrieval score close to the 0.25 coin-flip line on forecasting questions (GPT-4-1106 .208, others .215-.268 in Halawi; GPT-4 .20 not distinguishable from .25 in Schoenegger and Park, N=23; Phan base-LM ensembles mostly worse than .25). Bench to the Future finds all no-evidence models below .25, so the level depends on the question mix.
agent_test: Use .25 and a base-rate forecast as the two floors for every class; report plain-model Brier on the same items as the scaffold.

claim: Scaffolds with retrieval and reasoning move LLM forecasts about .03 Brier closer to the crowd but not past it: Halawi system .179 vs crowd .149 (N=914 test questions); plain models .206-.208. Phan's ReAct agent ensemble reached .169 vs humans .172 on a small set, and its base-LM ensemble did not improve.
agent_test: Equal-token test: plain model vs scaffold, Brier on resolved items, bootstrap CI; need enough items for a .007 difference (SE about .002-.003 at N=914).

claim: In Halawi's ablations retrieval mattered more than fine-tuning or prompt search (neither: .206; no fine-tune: .186; full .179), but the gaps of .003-.007 are near the standard errors and each ablation was run once.
agent_test: Repeat ablations with several seeds on our own scaffold components before keeping any element.

claim: Halawi's system beat the crowd where the crowd was unsure (.199 vs .246 for crowd forecasts .3-.7) but lost where the crowd was near 0 or 1, because it rarely outputs low probabilities (authors blame safety training; untested). Direction of bias varies elsewhere: Schoenegger et al. saw yes-bias (mean 57.35%), Pratt et al. a low-probability bias. Gap-search note: hedging toward the market or the middle shows up in Prophet Arena and the 2026 World Cup agents (under-confident top picks), but KalshiBench and LEAP's one-shot arm show over-confidence. No source tests an extremise step or a full-range instruction on held-out items.
agent_test: Plot predicted probability against outcome for each model and prompt on the same items; check whether the extreme bins (under 0.1, over 0.9) are populated and whether a push-to-extremes recalibration improves held-out Brier.

claim: Averaging an LLM forecast with the human crowd beats either: S&P blend .13 vs LLM .20 and crowd .07 (N=23); Silicon crowd averaging beat the models' own updated forecasts (GPT-4 .13 vs .14); Halawi found averaging best in every setting.
agent_test: No human crowd in our agent; the analogue is averaging two different-model forecasts at equal tokens (G4 limits same-model gains).

claim: Ensembling several different LLMs approached a 925-person human crowd on 31 questions (LLM .20, human .19, equivalence only within .081), yet Phan's base-LM ensemble gave no gain over the best single model. Small N and wide equivalence bounds.
agent_test: Compare median of 3 different models vs best single model at equal tokens on 100+ resolved items.

claim: Against superforecasters, top LLMs lag: 200-question subset superforecasters .096, public .121, Claude 3.5 Sonnet .122 (best LLM without crowd values .136); with combination questions .076, .096, GPT-4o .130. (Evidence line a23 had mixed up these two sets; corrected.) Top LLMs saw market crowd values. Update 2025-26: on the tournament board the gap shrank to .02 (Oct 2025: superforecasters .081, GPT-4.5 .101) and .017 (Mar 2026: .086 vs .103), with market prices given to the models; Good Judgment reports a wider gap on market questions (Brier Index 80.3 vs 75.8).
agent_test: Use ForecastBench-style unresolved questions as an external yardstick; do not compare our Brier to these numbers unless question mix matches.

claim: The ForecastBench extrapolation to superforecaster parity (Arena 1406, CI 1346-1633; 6.49e26 FLOP, CI 9.69e25-8.65e28) rests on about 10 models, R2 .47 and .41, p=.046, so it is a weak forecast. Update: FRI parity extrapolation moved from Nov 2026 (CI Dec 2025 to Jan 2028) to March 2027 by Brier and May 2027 by Brier Index (CI Apr 2026 to May 2028); authors call the shift a modelling artefact.
agent_test: None for the agent; keep as context only.

claim: Logical-consistency violations on related questions can be computed without outcomes and correlate with later Brier, but only some checks carry signal: conditional checks reach 0.69-0.92, negation is +0.60/+0.67 on scraped questions yet -0.36/-0.13 on NewsAPI, aggregate 0.85 (frequentist, scraped) and 0.49 (arbitrage). Part of the link is that better models are both more consistent and more accurate. Gap-search note: a second analysis on the same Paleka cliques finds that the size of incoherence predicts which bets lose most (CV AUC .775) and that negation and paraphrase checks carry little (Platt+JCD gain -4% and -1% vs -21% and -37% for and/or).
agent_test: Compute conditional-consistency violations for our agent on 50 question pairs and see if they predict next-batch Brier by class.

claim: Training with a Brier-style reward produces calibrated verbalized confidence: Damani HotpotQA ECE 0.37 to 0.03 (in-domain), Turtel 14B ECE .062 with Brier .190 on 1,265 Polymarket questions (still .039 worse than the market price), Leng reward calibration cut ECE by over 50% in DPO. Needs weight updates.
agent_test: Out of scope for a scaffold (no training); use only as proof that calibration is learnable from a graded record.

claim: More reasoning does not help calibration or forecast Brier: reasoning models are overconfident (above 85% on wrong answers) and more so at higher effort; thinking mode did not improve Claude Sonnet 4 on pastcasting (.1560 vs .1597, p=.53). Introspection helped o3-Mini and R1 but hurt Claude 3.7 Sonnet. Gap-search note: KalshiBench found extended reasoning (GPT-5.2-XHigh, 26 times more tokens) gave Brier .433 vs .227 for Claude Opus 4.5; an 8B forecaster's free reasoning added only +1.9 points accuracy over forced answering.
agent_test: Compare Brier at short vs long reasoning caps at equal tokens on resolved items.

claim: Component and calibration estimates from a small class record are unreliable; about 1,000 graded items were needed to learn a calibrator (Kapoor), and Halawi's isotonic/binning recalibration gave no gain on an already well-calibrated system (RMS error .42 vs crowd .38). Gap-search note: a learned classifier needs about 1,000 items (Kapoor), but a 2-parameter Platt fit on about 30% of a few hundred items removed 99% of a large reliability term (Kotawala). Power analysis: about 350 independent resolved items to see a .02 Brier edge, 1,400 for .01 (Foresight Arena, analytic).
agent_test: Report intervals and minimum counts per class; do not recalibrate classes with fewer than about 100 resolved items.

claim: Backtests of forecasters leak: date-restricted search returns hindsight pages and logically implied answers inflate scores. Pastcasting needs down-weighting of correlated questions (effective N 178.8). Unresolved questions (ForecastBench) avoid leaks.
agent_test: Score only on items that resolved after the prompt and tools were frozen; log freeze dates in S9.

claim: Users trust long LLM explanations more than the model's confidence warrants; matching explanation wording to true confidence narrows the calibration and discrimination gaps (model AUC .75-.78 vs participants .54-.60).
agent_test: Not a Brier test: show stated probability in plain text with every answer and check whether human reliance improves.

claim: Chain-of-thought before stating confidence did not improve verbalized calibration (gpt-3.5 TriviaQA 2-stage top-1 .131 vs 1-stage .068), and an 8B forecaster's stated confidence barely changed whether or not it reasoned first (Spearman .90 between forced and free; same answer on 67% of questions).
agent_test: Compare confidence stated before vs after reasoning on the same items.

claim: A structured scaffold (decomposition into sub-questions, per-evidence likelihoods, base rate plus odds updates) lowers Brier, and the data that exist say it works through reliability rather than resolution: sub-question decomposition took calibration .026 to .008 and refinement .091 to .083 (Brier .141 to .132, n=500). At matched tokens a likelihood-aggregation scaffold (LEAP) cut ECE .147 to .088 and Brier .250 to .206 against a two-sample monolithic arm.
agent_test: Log REL and RES separately for each scaffold arm on the same resolved items; test whether the scaffold lowers REL without lowering RES.

claim: Superforecaster gap on ForecastBench is now about .02 Brier, not .05: tournament board Oct 2025 .081 vs GPT-4.5 .101; Mar 2026 .086 vs .103 (ensemble and Grok 4.20 Preview). Models see market prices on market questions and GPT-4.5 correlates .994 with them. Good Judgment reports a wider gap on market questions (Brier Index 80.3 vs 75.8) and a thin human panel.
agent_test: Always record whether the market or crowd price was in the prompt; do not compare a copy-the-price score with a no-price score.

claim: Frontier chat models without the market price are close to coin-flip on hard markets: soft-Brier .256 for Claude Opus 4.5 on 265 Polymarket questions (.281 on the 104 the crowd had not decided, crowd .232); KalshiBench BSS vs base rate +.057 for the best of five models, -.799 for the extended-reasoning one. Showing the price is worth .04-.075 Brier and models then converge on it (r .97-.99 on World Cup matches).
agent_test: Report BSS against the class base rate next to Brier, and tag each S9 entry price-visible or not.

claim: Brier and log score rank forecasters alike within noise on a real record, and ECE can rank them the other way: log vs Brier rewards gave test Brier .1653 vs .1648 on 965 items against a three-seed spread of .0032; in the World Cup run the best top-pick ECE (Gemini .068) had the worst Brier.
agent_test: Log both Brier and log score per class; treat differences under about .005 Brier as ties; never rank by ECE alone.

claim: For tasks with exact answers, self-reported effort and ability ratings beat stated confidence at predicting failure (average AUROC gain 10.1 and 8.4 points, 12 LLMs, 38 tasks) with lower calibration error and higher resolution; ratings were scaled to [0,1] and are not true probabilities. No source scores a pass/fail-check-to-probability map by Brier.
agent_test: Test on our tasks: log an effort-style rating next to stated confidence and compare AUROC and Brier of each against the check outcome.

claim: Class-level numbers need many items: detecting a .02 Brier edge at 80% power takes about 350 independent resolved predictions, .01 takes about 1,400, .05 about 56 (analytic, base rate .5). A 21-case pilot gave AUC .756 with interval .471 to .980.
agent_test: Show a class-level calibration or ranking in S9 only after about 100 items for coarse flags and about 350 for any claim of a .02 difference.

claim: Post-hoc Platt scaling helps when raw stated probabilities are badly calibrated and not when they already are: raw K-sample means REL .0357 to .0004 after Platt (Brier .228 to .185, 30% fit / 70% test); Halawi's already-calibrated system gained nothing from binning or isotonic; per-model Platt on ForecastBench matched the strongest single model in 7 of 16 groups and the best pooled pair in 2 of 16.
agent_test: Fit a 2-parameter map per class only when measured REL is above about .01 on at least 100 items; check on held-out items.

claim: Retrieved news can move a class's calibration without any change to the model: five injected articles flipped 69-73% of forecasts across 0.5 and raised Brier from .18 to .37 in three 7-8B retrieval forecasters; a notebook or memory layer lowered Brier for 6 of 12 models (none significant) and raised it significantly for two.
agent_test: Log retrieval source and date per S9 entry; re-check class calibration after any change to tools or sources.
